Field studies on the Three-lined rainbowfish (Stethojulis trilineata) provide detailed insights into its early life history, particularly under controlled thermal conditions. At a stable water temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], the period from fertilization to eclosion is remarkably brief. The developing embryos, which begin as small, transparent, pelagic eggs, complete their incubation and hatch after approximately 3.6 days [ab = approximately 3.6 days] at a temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C]. This rapid hatching rate, occurring at this specific temperature, is characteristic of many tropical wrasses that inhabit warm, stable reef environments, presumably reducing the vulnerability of the egg stage to predation and physical disturbance. Upon emergence, the newly hatched larva possesses a minimal body mass, with an initial wet weight at birth calculated to be roughly 0.000268 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.000268 grams]. This extraordinarily low mass reflects the tiny size of the fertilized ovum, which has an estimated diameter of about 0.8 millimeters, and marks the beginning of a highly vulnerable planktonic larval phase where the individual must quickly transition from relying on its endogenous yolk reserves to capturing its own prey.

As the larvae of Stethojulis trilineata develop and grow through the pelagic phase, they undergo a significant metamorphosis before settling onto the reef. Following the completion of the larval-juvenile transition, the young fish enter a period of rapid somatic growth. Individual growth trajectories, derived from extensive field collections and otolith microchemistry analyses, indicate that this species reaches a maximum or ultimate total length of approximately 16.5 centimeters [Li = approximately 16.5 centimeters] as a fully grown adult. This asymptotic size is typical for a small-to-medium-sized member of the Labridae family inhabiting coral-rich habitats. Along this growth curve, a critical developmental milestone is the attainment of sexual maturity. The total length at which half the population is estimated to have reached puberty is recorded as 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters]. This length-based metric is particularly useful for fisheries management, as it provides a clear, non-invasive proxy for identifying the size at which individuals become capable of contributing to the next generation, thereby informing minimum size limits for capture in regions where the species is targeted.

Body mass is another fundamental trait that defines the life history strategy of the Three-lined rainbowfish, scaling predictably with length according to the species' length-weight relationship. At the onset of reproductive maturity, corresponding to the total length of 9 centimeters, the estimated wet weight at puberty is approximately 9.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 9.3 grams], a modest mass reflecting the size at which gonadal development commences in this species. As the individual continues to grow toward its ultimate size of 16.5 centimeters, it attains a considerably larger body mass. The ultimate wet weight, representing the maximum adult body mass, is calculated to be around 60.8 grams [Wwi = around 60.8 grams]. This nearly seven-fold increase in mass from the point of puberty to the asymptotic size underscores the significant post-maturation growth that continues in this iteroparous species. This pattern suggests that larger, older individuals may enjoy disproportionately higher fecundity and reproductive success, a common theme among reef fishes where body size is a strong predictor of egg output and competitive dominance.

Under the same thermal regime of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], the spawning population exhibits a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of approximately 10% [GSI = approximately 10%]. This lifespan is comparable to that reported for Centrolabrus exoletus, suggesting a common pattern within certain labrid lineages.

The early developmental timing of Stethojulis trilineata is tightly linked to ambient temperature, a relationship that has significant ecological consequences in the variable thermal landscape of coral reef environments. The exceedingly rapid embryonic development, culminating in hatching after just 3.6 days [ab = 3.6 days] at 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C], stands in stark contrast to the much longer incubation periods observed in temperate or cold-water fish species. This accelerated pace compresses the window of vulnerability for the egg stage. Given this brief incubation, a total lifespan of approximately eight years [am = approximately eight years] represents a substantial investment in post-embryonic life, allowing for multiple reproductive seasons at a temperature of 28.7 °C [T = 28.7 °C].
